Three custom dice, A, B, and C, are designed so that A beats B more than half the time, and B beats C more than half the time (in a roll-off, higher number wins). Must A also beat C more than half the time?
choices: No such set of three dice can actually exist
No — dice can be built so that C actually beats A more often than not (nontransitive dice)
Yes, but only if all three dice have six sides

questions.q: In the 'Monty Fall' variant of the Monty Hall problem, the host doesn't know what's behind the doors. You pick door 1 out of 3. The host randomly opens one of the other two doors, and by chance it reveals a goat. Given this, what is the probability the car is behind your original door versus the remaining closed door?
choices: 1/3 for your door, 2/3 for the other, just like the classic problem
You should always switch because it can't hurt your odds
1/2 for each — switching gives no advantage here
2/3 if you switch, same as the classic Monty Hall problem

questions.q: In Penney's Game, Player 1 picks a sequence of coin-flip outcomes (like HHT), then Player 2 picks a different sequence after seeing it. Coins are flipped repeatedly until one sequence appears first. Can Player 2 always choose a sequence giving better than 50% odds of winning, no matter what Player 1 picked?
choices: Only if the sequences chosen are the same length as each other
No, Player 1 always has the advantage since they choose first
No, the game is always exactly fair at 50/50 odds
Yes — a well-chosen reply sequence always gives Player 2 better than 50% odds

questions.q: A group of students scores unusually high on a test, largely due to lucky guessing as well as skill. If they retake a similar test, their average score will most likely:
choices: Drop back closer to the group's true average ability, due to regression to the mean
Stay exactly the same, since ability doesn't change
Drop to the lowest possible score, as a correction
Rise even higher, since they've proven they're skilled

questions.q: In Zeno's paradox, Achilles races a tortoise that gets a head start. Each time Achilles reaches the tortoise's last position, the tortoise has crept a bit further ahead — seemingly forever. In reality, does Achilles ever catch the tortoise?
choices: No — since there are infinitely many steps, it necessarily takes infinite time
No — Zeno proved motion itself is mathematically impossible
It depends on the tortoise's exact starting speed relative to Achilles
Yes — the infinite sequence of time intervals sums to a finite total, so he catches up in finite time

questions.q: A fair coin has just landed heads 6 times in a row. What is the probability that the next flip is heads?
choices: It depends on how many times it landed heads before that
More than 1/2, because it's on a streak
Less than 1/2, because tails is due

questions.q: Hospital A has a 90% overall survival rate and Hospital B has an 80% overall survival rate. Yet when patients are split into mild and severe cases, Hospital B has the higher survival rate in BOTH categories. How is this possible?
choices: Overall survival rate cannot be computed from category rates
It is mathematically impossible — the claim must be false
Hospital A treats a much larger proportion of mild, low-risk cases than Hospital B (Simpson's paradox)

questions.q: In a city, 85% of cabs are Green and 15% are Blue. A witness says the hit-and-run cab was Blue. In tests under similar conditions, the witness correctly identifies each color 80% of the time and misidentifies it 20% of the time. What is the probability the cab was actually Blue?

choices: None — a hole has no dirt in it
